info.title: RouteLens Lite API
info.description: A simple IPv4 routing table analyzer for a college project

get.description:
Check if the virtual router lab is available and ready.

Returns lab status, router interfaces, routing table, and any blockers.

Note: This endpoint reports on the rl260-* lab (rl260-client, rl260-router, rl260-server).
The application does not provide a method to create this lab; it must exist beforehand.

post.summary: Simulate packet transmission through virtual router
post.description:
Simulate a packet transmission through the virtual router.

Transmits a real packet and captures it for verification.
Returns verification details including TTL decrement, checksum, and route matching
with provenance (observed/inferred/simulated/unknown) for each check.

Note: This endpoint requires the rl260-* lab (rl260-client, rl260-router, rl260-server)
to exist and be accessible. The application does not provide a method to create this lab.

get.description: List all available scenarios.

schema.title: Response List Scenarios Api Scenarios Get

get.description: Full definition of one scenario.

post.description:
Trace a packet from a source node to a destination address.

The trace is produced by the same scenario definition that the lab builder
uses, so simulation and reality stay comparable.

Passing a workspace id traces the edited copy, so a route change is
reflected in the next simulation.

put.description:
Replace the static routes of a node.

Works on a copy so that a malformed request cannot corrupt the shared
scenario registry. The updated scenario is returned along with a
workspace id; pass that id to the trace endpoint to see the effect of
the edit.

Toggle a link between UP and DOWN in an isolated workspace.

Identifies the link by its endpoints (a and b in either direction),
updates only a copy of the scenario in a workspace, and returns the
updated workspace id. The shared scenario definition is never corrupted.

post.description:
Create the namespaces for a scenario.

Defaults to a dry run that only reports the commands. Executing for real
requires root and is refused otherwise.
Remove the namespaces for a scenario.

Compare the simulated trace with a real probe from the lab.

When the lab is unavailable the agreement field is null; no result is
invented to make the comparison look conclusive.

get.description:
Build a topology graph for a scenario from two kinds of evidence.

The scenario contributes simulated devices and links. The real host
contributes observed interfaces, routes and neighbours, plus the
relationships inferred between them.

Every node and edge carries its own provenance so the client can
colour them differently and the user can tell measured from modelled.
List the guided exercises.
The full explanation and instructions for one exercise.

post.description:
Check whether an exercise has been completed.

The check runs the real routing engine against the scenario, so an
exercise is only complete when the engine's own output satisfies it.

A workspace may be supplied so the student's route edits are the
ones that get checked.

get.description: List the exercises that work on the host's own routing table.
The full explanation and instructions for one host exercise.

post.description:
Check a host exercise against the student's own routing table.

The table is read from the kernel with `ip -j route show` and is
OBSERVED. The conclusion drawn from it is INFERRED. The two are reported
separately and never merged.

When the machine's table does not have what the exercise needs, the
result says so plainly and points at what the student could look at
instead. It does not fall back to a modelled table, and it does not
pretend the exercise succeeded.

get.description: Every discovery request that has been made, in order.

post.description:
Check a scope and describe it, without probing anything.

This is the step before confirmation: it shows exactly what would be
probed so the operator can agree to it.

schema.title: Response Preview Scope Api Discovery Scope Post

post.description:
Run an authorised discovery.

The scope is validated, then the operator's confirmation is checked.
Without a matching confirmation nothing is probed, and the refusal
is recorded.

A run probes real addresses with real packets, so it is rate limited
per client. The limit is its own, not the diagnostic one, so a burst
of lookups cannot use up a student's discovery allowance.

Ask a running scan to stop.

A scan id that is not running is reported as such rather than being
recorded as cancelled. Claiming a cancellation that never happened
would be a false account of what the machine did.

get.description:
Build a report of what was observed.

The report records the evidence behind each claim, where it came
from, when it was collected, and what could not be established.

Set format=markdown for a plain-text report suitable for a file.

post.description:
Build a report incorporating the user's active experiment.

Captures the exact scenario, packet trace, failure diagnostics,
and before-and-after comparison from the active user session.

Analyze a PCAP capture file.

The file is provided as base64-encoded bytes in the request body.
No file is written to disk - parsing happens entirely in memory.

Args:
    request: PcapAnalyzeRequest with filename and base64 data
    
Returns:
    PcapAnalyzeResponse with analysis results or error details
    
Supported formats:
    - Classic PCAP (link type 1 - Ethernet)
    - PCAPNG (detected but not parsed)
    
Errors:
    - 400: Invalid base64, missing filename, empty body
    - 413: File exceeds 32 MB limit
    - 200 with parsed=false: Unsupported format, truncated file, invalid magic

Explain what the editable routing table would do.

This is the table the Route Lookup works against, not the host's
kernel table. The same analysis machinery that explains the kernel's
table is used here, so both are described in the same words.

Two claims are kept apart:
- The table is what the student built. It is MODELLED.
- The explanation is INFERRED from it.

Args:
    destination: Optional destination address to explain. When omitted,
        the table's own destinations are explained.

Returns:
    A report with the analysis for each destination, the candidates
    each route beat, any shadowing found, and the limits of the answer.

Errors:
    - 400: The destination is not a valid IP address

post.description:
Trace the path a packet would take from source to destination through the routing table.

This endpoint traces the packet's path hop by hop through the routing table,
showing each routing decision made at each hop.

Each hop is a decision made by the router holding the packet at that moment,
using that router's own table. The teaching table describes one router, so a
journey that reaches another router stops there with the action
'unresolved_next_hop': the packet was forwarded, but that router's table is
not part of this one, so its forwarding cannot be worked out. The Scenario Lab
traces the full path through a network where every router has a table.

The action on each hop is one of:
  forward             - the router handed the packet to a next hop
  deliver             - the packet reached the destination
  drop                - the packet was discarded: no route, or the hop limit ran out
  loop                - the packet came back to a router it had already been at
  unresolved_next_hop - the packet was forwarded to a router whose table is unknown
  error               - the request, or a routing table, could not be read

Nothing is transmitted. The journey is calculated from a routing table, which
is what the response's 'provenance' field says.

Args:
    request: PacketJourneyRequest with source and destination IPs

Returns:
    PacketJourneyResponse with hop-by-hop trace

get.description:
Get real network interfaces from the host system.

Uses `ip -j addr show` to collect interface information including:
- Interface name, index, state, MTU
- MAC address
- IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and networks
- Interface flags

Returns:
    CollectionResult with list of InterfaceInfo objects

Get real routing table from the host system.

Uses `ip -j route show` to collect routing entries including:
- Destination prefix
- Gateway (next hop)
- Interface
- Metric
- Protocol
- Scope

The IPv4 and IPv6 tables are separate tables in the kernel, so the
family is a parameter. The default is IPv4, which is what the table
most viewers expect; pass `ip_version=ipv6` to read the other one.

Args:
    ip_version: Which table to read. "ipv4" (the default) or "ipv6".

Returns:
    CollectionResult with list of RouteInfo objects

Analyse the real routing table and explain what it would do.

Reads the host's routing table with `ip -j route show` (or `ip -j -6
route show` for IPv6), converts it into the same model the routing
engine uses, and then explains, for a destination, which route would
win and which candidates it beat.

Two different claims are kept apart here:
- The routing table is OBSERVED. It was read from the kernel.
- The explanation is INFERRED. It is a reading of the table.

No packet is transmitted and no route is changed.

Args:
    destination: Optional destination address to explain. When omitted, a
        set of interesting destinations is chosen: this host's own
        addresses, the default route's gateway, and a public address.
    ip_version: Which routing table to read, "ipv4" or "ipv6". The kernel
        keeps the two separately. When a destination is given, its own
        family decides, because an IPv6 destination says nothing about
        the IPv4 table.

Returns:
    RouteAnalysisReport with the analysis, the candidates each route beat,
    any shadowing found, and the limits of the analysis.

Errors:
    - 400: The destination is not a valid IP address, or the family is
      neither ipv4 nor ipv6
    - 500: The routing table could not be read

Get real ARP/IPv6 neighbor cache from the host system.

Uses `ip -j neigh show` to collect neighbor entries including:
- IP address
- Interface
- MAC address (if available)
- Neighbor state (REACHABLE, STALE, etc.)
- Router flag
- A reverse DNS name, when one could be looked up

The name is looked up with a reverse DNS query, which is INFERRED, while
the address itself is OBSERVED. The two are reported separately. A
neighbour with no PTR record is reported as having no name, not with
its own address repeated back as if it were a hostname.

The lookup is bounded: it has a short timeout, it runs concurrently, and
only a limited number of neighbours are looked up at all. A neighbour
list always comes back complete, with names absent if they could not be
found.

Args:
    resolve_names: Whether to look up reverse DNS names. Turning this off
        avoids the DNS traffic entirely.

Returns:
    CollectionResult with list of NeighborInfo objects

Get all network information in a single request.

Collects interfaces, routes, and neighbors in parallel.

Returns:
    Object with interfaces, routes, and neighbors CollectionResults

post.description:
Resolve a hostname to IP addresses using the system's DNS resolver.

Uses the system's DNS resolver via asyncio.getaddrinfo() with configurable timeout.
Supports both IPv4 (A) and IPv6 (AAAA) records.

Args:
    request: DnsResolveRequest with hostname, timeout, and ipv6 options

Returns:
    DnsResolveResponse with resolved addresses, latency, and any error

Raises:
    HTTPException: 400 for invalid hostname, 429 when rate limited, 500 for internal errors

Check connectivity to a target using ICMP ping or TCP connect.

Supports both ICMP ping (host reachability) and TCP connect (port reachability).
Uses system ping command for ICMP and asyncio.open_connection for TCP.

Args:
    request: ConnectivityRequest with target, protocol, and options

Returns:
    ConnectivityResponse with reachability, latency, and any error

Raises:
    HTTPException: 400 for invalid input, 408 for timeout, 429 when rate limited, 500 for internal errors

Perform traceroute to a target using the system traceroute command.

Traces the path packets take to reach a destination by sending packets
with incrementing TTL values and collecting ICMP time-exceeded responses.

Args:
    request: TracerouteRequest with target and options

Returns:
    TracerouteResponse with list of hops, each containing TTL, address, hostname, RTT

Raises:
    HTTPException: 400 for invalid input, 408 for timeout, 429 when rate limited, 500 for internal errors

PacketHopResponse.title: PacketHopResponse
PacketHopResponse.description:
One hop of a packet journey.

The fields are exactly the ones the interface renders. A field that
does not apply to this hop is left out of the response entirely,
rather than sent as null, so the shape of the data says what
happened.

Attributes:
    hop_number: Which hop this is, counting from 1
    current_device: The device making the decision at this hop
    destination_ip: The destination the packet is travelling towards
    action: One of PACKET_JOURNEY_ACTIONS
    explanation: A plain-language account of the decision
    matched_route: The route that was selected, when one was
    next_hop_ip: The address the packet was handed to
    egress_interface: The interface the packet left by

PacketJourneyResponse.title: PacketJourneyResponse
PacketJourneyResponse.description:
Response model for packet journey trace.

The journey is worked out from a routing table. No packet is sent,
so the answer is a calculated decision rather than an observation of
traffic, and `provenance` says so.

Attributes:
    source_ip: The address the packet started from
    destination_ip: The address the packet was heading for
    hops: Each forwarding decision, in order
    success: Whether the packet was shown reaching the destination
    error: Why the journey did not reach the destination, if it did not
    failure_code: Structured failure code, or null on successful delivery
    provenance: How this journey was arrived at
